name: stage11s_correctness_pairs_v1
evidence: author-written good/bad questions on four cases that are NOT in the benchmark and not paraphrases of the known failures; same author as the rules, so a sanity set, not independent evidence
note: each bad question carries exactly one defect, named in `why`; the good ones must stay accepted

items.question: What is a deadlock?
items.answer: Two threads each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can continue.
items.reference: A deadlock happens when threads wait on each other in a cycle. Lock ordering prevents it: every thread takes locks in the same agreed order, so no cycle can form. A timeout lets a thread give up and retry instead of waiting forever.
good: How would taking the locks in the same order in every thread stop that cycle forming?
What would a timeout change for a thread that is already waiting on a held lock?

bad.q: How does a locked lock behave when the lock is actually unlocked?
How do deadlocks compare with those found in lock ordering?
bad.why: circular contrast: lock ordering is not a rival kind of deadlock

bad.q: How do two threads each hold a lock the other needs when neither can continue?
How would lock ordering help the threads that hold the longest locks?
bad.why: invented qualifier: no longest lock anywhere

bad.q: How would lock ordering help here, and what would a timeout change?

items.question: What does a cache-control header do?
items.answer: It tells the browser how long it may reuse a response before asking again.
items.reference: max-age gives the number of seconds a response may be reused. Revalidation asks the server whether a stored copy is still good, usually with an ETag. A stale response is one kept past its lifetime, which a client may still use while it revalidates.
good: How would a client check with the server that a stored copy is still good?
What would a browser do with a copy kept past its lifetime?

bad.q: How does a fresh response behave once the response is stale?
How does revalidation compare with those found in max-age?
How does it tell the browser how long it may reuse a response before asking again?
Which header would you set for the shortest possible response?

items.question: What is a p-value?
items.answer: It is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis holds.
items.reference: The significance level is the threshold chosen before the test, against which the p-value is compared. Multiple comparisons inflate the chance of a spurious result, because every extra test gets its own opportunity to look surprising. Effect size says how large the difference is, which a p-value alone never shows.
good: How would running twenty tests change your reading of a single surprising result?
What would you still not know about a difference from its p-value alone?

bad.q: How does a significant result behave when the result is insignificant?
How does a p-value compare with those found in significance level?
How is it the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis holds?
How would the effect size matter for the smallest observed difference?
How would the threshold matter, and which effect size would worry you?
bad.why: two questions (not detected: the second interrogative is separated from its verb by a noun phrase; see the report)

items.question: What does git rebase do?
items.answer: It replays your commits on top of another branch so the history stays linear.
items.reference: A merge commit keeps both lines of development and records where they joined. Rewritten history gives every replayed commit a new identifier, so anyone who already has the old ones sees a divergence. On a shared branch that divergence forces colleagues to reconcile their copies.
good: What would a colleague who already pulled those commits see afterwards?
How would keeping the join point instead change what the history shows?

bad.q: How does a shared branch behave when the branch is unshared?
How does rebasing compare with those found in rewritten history?
How does it replay your commits on top of another branch so the history stays linear?
Which approach helps on the largest branch?
